recorded: 15 March and 18 April 1921, Camden, New Jersey (the issued take was made on 18 April)
question: What does a four-minute acoustic disc keep of a work built on a hymn and its struggle?
intro: A 1921 acoustic disc fits Finlandia onto one side: an agitated opening, a hymn and a loud close. Listen through the surface noise to how the band is balanced, and to the moment the hymn arrives.

cues.title: Half of a work, on one side
cues.text: The Victor disc holds only about four minutes of music. Wikipedia gives a typical performance as seven and a half to nine minutes, so the work is abridged here. Where the cuts fall is not documented; this note makes no claim about bars.
cues.evidence: DAHR lists matrix C-24988 as a 12-inch master issued on Victor 74698; the file lasts 4:06 (245.8 s). Typical duration of 7½–9 minutes: Wikipedia’s article on Finlandia. The report shows music from about 0:05 to about 3:52 and no way to identify cut bars.

cues.title: Fast, agitated, loud
cues.text: The opening seconds are quick and loud for an acoustic disc: from −17 dB at 0:05 the level rises to about −11 dB, with four to five attacks a second. Wikipedia describes most of the piece as turbulent music of national struggle.
cues.evidence: Relative level −28.9 dB (0:00), −16.7 (0:05), −10.8 (0:10), −10.8 (0:15), −12.6 (0:20); onsets per second 4.6, 4.8, 3.2, 5.0, 4.0 over 0:00–0:20. “Rousing and turbulent music, evoking the national struggle”: Wikipedia’s article on Finlandia.

cues.title: A protest in disguise
cues.text: Sibelius wrote it in 1899 for the Press Celebrations, a covert protest against growing Russian censorship; it was the last of seven pieces accompanying a tableau of Finnish history. He revised it in 1900, and the revised version was performed in Helsinki on 2 July 1900.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s article on Finlandia (lead and “History”): Press Celebrations of 1899, covert protest against censorship, seventh and last piece for a tableau, revision in 1900. The Sibelius Society of Finland’s page (https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_finlandia.htm): the revised version’s first public performance on 2 July 1900, “possibly earlier”, by the Helsinki Philharmonic Society under Robert Kajanus; the earlier tableau music was first performed on 4 November 1899. The note sits over the loud opening (−8 to −13 dB, 0:30–0:50).

cues.title: Listen to the horn
cues.text: In 1921 the orchestra played into a horn, not a microphone. Victor’s ledger for the March session, whose takes were destroyed, lists a small band; the forces of the April take issued here are not confirmed. Listen for how the balance of strings, winds and brass sounds through the horn.
cues.evidence: DAHR matrix record: instrumentation “7 first violins, 5 second violins, 3 violas, 2 cellos, 4 string basses, harp, 3 oboes, 3 clarinets, 2 bassoons, 2 trumpets, 3 trombones, 2 tubas, and traps”, taken from Victor ledgers for 15 March 1921 and “not confirmed for later takes”; takes 1 and 2 (15 March) and take 3 (18 April) were destroyed and take 4 (18 April) is the issued master, so the listed band is not identified as the one heard here. The Internet Archive item gives “Technical Notes: Acoustic”. The balance remark is a general listening suggestion, not a measured claim.

cues.title: The hymn arrives
cues.text: At about 1:24 the level drops by about eight decibels, to −15.6 dB, and by another five by 1:30. The key reading moves to A♭ major, where the Finlandia hymn sits. Sibelius wrote the tune himself; it is not a folk melody.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 1:24 (novelty 0.57); relative level −7.7 dB (1:20), −15.6 (1:25), −20.8 (1:30); onsets per second 2.6 (1:20), 2.2 (1:25), 1.6 (1:30); local key A♭ major (r 0.50–0.70) at 1:25–2:45 (confirmation only). That the hymn is Sibelius’s own and often wrongly called a folk melody: Wikipedia’s article on Finlandia.

cues.title: A tune with many lives
cues.text: The words that now go with the hymn were written in 1940 by Veikko Antero Koskenniemi. With other words the tune is an English hymn, a Welsh patriotic hymn and an Italian evangelical one, and it was the national anthem of Biafra. Sibelius reworked it as a stand-alone piece.
cues.evidence: The Sibelius Society of Finland’s page (https://sibelius.klubi.fi/english/musiikki/ork_finlandia.htm): Koskenniemi’s words commissioned in September 1940 by the Laulu-Miehet choir and first performed on 7 December 1940 (Wikipedia gives 1941, which the Society’s chronology contradicts). Wikipedia’s article on Finlandia (“Derivative works”): Sibelius’s later reworking of the hymn as a stand-alone piece, the English, Welsh and Italian adaptations, the Biafran anthem. The note sits in the quieter hymn (−14 to −20 dB, 1:50–2:25).

cues.title: Four takes, one survives
cues.text: Victor made four takes of the work, two on 15 March 1921 and two on 18 April, in Camden, New Jersey. The first three were destroyed. The fourth is the master from which this side, Victor 74698, was issued.
cues.evidence: DAHR matrix C-24988: takes 1 and 2 on 15 March 1921 (destroyed), take 3 on 18 April 1921 (destroyed), take 4 on 18 April 1921 (master), issued on Victor 74698. The note sits in the steady hymn (−12 to −16 dB, 2:35–2:50).

cues.title: The hymn gathers force
cues.text: From about 3:00 the level rises through −12 dB to −6.9 dB at 3:15 and −4.7 dB at 3:25, the loudest window of the side. This closing stretch holds high for half a minute.

cues.title: The music stops
cues.text: At about 3:52 the music stops and the level drops from about −15 dB to −34 dB by 3:55. The last fourteen seconds of the file stay below −28 dB. The strongest boundary of the whole side falls here.
cues.evidence: Strongest boundary at 3:52 (novelty 1.00); relative level −15.2 dB (3:50), −33.6 (3:55), −30.9 (4:00), −28.3 dB (4:05); the quietest 5-second windows are 3:55, 4:00, 0:00 and 4:05. The report cannot say what the low-level sound is.

transitions.title: Agitation drops away; a hymn begins
transitions.how: After more than a minute of loud music, with four to five attacks a second until about 0:55, the level falls by about eight decibels at 1:24 and the playing grows sparser. The key estimate moves from E♭ to A♭ major, the key of the hymn. This is the central contrast of Finlandia: struggle gives way to a broad tune that Sibelius wrote himself. In this abridged version the join may also be a cut; the disc does not say.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 1:24 (novelty 0.57); relative level −7.7 dB (1:20), −15.6 (1:25), −20.8 (1:30); onsets per second 2.6 to 1.6; local key E♭ major (r 0.56–0.78) at 0:35–1:20, A♭ major (r 0.50–0.70) from 1:25 (confirmation only). The hymn’s origin: Wikipedia’s article.

transitions.title: The hymn grows to its loudest
transitions.how: After more than a minute and a half of hymn, the level climbs at about 3:00 from −12 dB towards −4.7 dB at 3:25, the loudest point of the side. The attacks pick up slightly and the sound fills out. Sibelius’s broad tune is carried to a closing climax instead of fading, and the disc ends soon after at about 3:52.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 3:00 (novelty 0.82); relative level −16.1 dB (2:50), −9.3 (2:55), −12.4 (3:00), −9.7 (3:10), −6.9 (3:15), −4.7 dB (3:25); onsets per second 1.8 (2:50) to 3.4 (3:10) and 4.0 (3:25); strongest boundary of the side at 3:52 (novelty 1.00).

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: DAHR gives Philadelphia Orchestra and Leopold Stokowski. The Internet Archive item credits “Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra”, a variant of the same ensemble’s name. DAHR’s instrumentation list (7 first violins, 5 second violins, 3 violas, 2 cellos, 4 basses, harp, 3 oboes, 3 clarinets, 2 bassoons, 2 trumpets, 3 trombones, 2 tubas, traps) comes from Victor ledgers for 15 March 1921 and is not confirmed for the issued take.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Abridged orchestral version; which passages are omitted is not documented
fields.note: The abridgement is inferred from the file’s length, 4:06, against a typical performance of 7½–9 minutes (Wikipedia), and from the disc being a single 12-inch side. DAHR and the Internet Archive do not describe the cut, and neither names an edition or cut scheme. This dossier does not locate cut bars.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 18 April 1921 (issued take 4); earlier takes 1–2 on 15 March 1921
fields.note: DAHR: takes 1 and 2 on 15 March 1921 and 3 on 18 April were destroyed; take 4 (18 April 1921) is the issued master. A bracketed [1921] is the date given for the issue on Victor 74698. Some listings give the earlier date for the first takes.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: DAHR gives Camden, New Jersey for every take.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: DAHR describes the object as Victor 74698, Red Seal 12-inch single-faced. Later issues on Victor 6366 and Gramophone Company DB-599 and 3-0662 are listed for the same matrix and take.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: The Internet Archive item also shows matrix and catalogue number 74698 and publisher “Victrola”.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The Internet Archive item shows 74698 as its matrix number; the Victor matrix is C-24988.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: George Blood, L.P. (digitisation (scanning centre), Great 78 Project)
fields.note: The item metadata names George Blood, L.P. as scanning centre and credits Robert Boggs with metadata and transfer entry and Kevin Coupe with cleaning (as Internet Archive user fields).

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item’s public date is 19 March 2021; that is the upload date, not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Digitised at 78 rpm with four styli (3.8, 2.3, 2.8 and 3.3 mil truncated conical); the preferred version was selected by an engineer at George Blood and copied to the friendly file name
fields.note: The item’s notes say the record was acoustic and that the other side was “not completed due to physical condition of disc”. The MP3 used here is the Internet Archive derivative of the 24-bit FLAC; no further processing is disclosed.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Sibelius died in 1957; in countries with a life-plus-70 term the composition remains in copyright until the end of 2027
fields.note: Computed from the composer’s life dates, given in DAHR’s MARC record as 1865–1957. The composition’s status in other territories is not assessed. The programme’s rule applies to the sound recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 2 — United States public domain: first published in 1921, before the 1926 cut-off.
fields.note: DAHR records the issue on Victor 74698 as [1921]; the brackets mean the year was supplied by the cataloguer, and no month of issue is recorded. The take issued was made on 18 April 1921, so publication followed that date. The Internet Archive item date is also 1921. The item has no licence URL and no non-commercial restriction in its metadata.

composer.born: 8 December 1865, Hämeenlinna, Grand Duchy of Finland
composer.epithet: A symphonist who let small figures gather into themes and movements change shape while their underlying pulse continued.
facts: Helsinki with Martin Wegelius, 1885–89 · Berlin with Albert Becker · Vienna with Robert Fuchs and Karl Goldmark
Ainola, designed by Lars Sonck near Lake Tuusula; the family moved there in 1904
Swedish at home; Finnish education and Finnish texts in Kullervo and Luonnotar
Seven numbered symphonies; violin concerto; tone poems, incidental music, songs and chamber works
composer.background:
Sibelius was born in 1865 in Hämeenlinna, when Finland was an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire. His family spoke Swedish, but he attended a Finnish-language school and encountered the Kalevala, Elias Lönnrot’s compilation of traditional epic poetry, in Finnish. The later national figure grew up between these cultures. His father, a doctor, died in 1868. Violin playing became the young Sibelius’s principal musical ambition, and family chamber music gave him an early practical knowledge of strings. He adopted the French form Jean from the visiting cards of a deceased uncle, replacing the familiar Janne professionally.

He entered the Helsinki Music Institute in 1885 after briefly beginning law studies. Martin Wegelius taught him composition; Ferruccio Busoni, then teaching piano in Helsinki, became a friend. Further study with Albert Becker in Berlin and Robert Fuchs and Karl Goldmark in Vienna extended his knowledge of Continental music. His hope of becoming a professional violin virtuoso did not survive an unsuccessful Vienna audition. The instrument nevertheless remained central to his melodic imagination: sustained notes against tremolando strings, rapid changes of register and the tension of a long line across the bow recur throughout the orchestral works.
